section.title: Technology and graphs
section.p: A graphing calculator or computer can draw in a second what would take minutes by hand. That speed is useful. It is also dangerous.
A screen does not show a function. It shows a sampled picture of a function in a chosen window.
The picture may be excellent. It may also miss a hole, hide a turn, smooth out an oscillation, or round away a small but important difference.
The right attitude is not distrust. It is partnership.

remark.title: Using technology wisely
remark.p: Use technology to see. Use mathematics to check.

subsection.title: Windows can lie
subsection.p: A graphing window is a rectangle:
subsection.md: x_{\min}\le x\le x_{\max}, \qquad y_{\min}\le y\le y_{\max}.
subsection.p: Anything outside that rectangle is invisible. The same function can look simple in one window and complicated in another.

The screen may not show the difference between h(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1} and \ell(x)=x+1. Algebra does.

warning.title: Window warning
warning.p: A graph can suggest: There may be a zero, a turn, a hole, or an asymptote.
It cannot by itself prove: There is exactly one, or none, or always.

subsection.title: Sampling can miss behavior
subsection.p: A computer cannot check infinitely many points. It samples finitely many input values, plots the corresponding output values, and connects or displays them.
Usually this works well. Sometimes it fails spectacularly.

statement.p: Oscillations appear in sound, light, vibration, and signal processing. Sampling matters.

warning.title: Sampling warning
warning.p: A graph drawn from samples is trustworthy only at the scale the sampling can see.

subsection.title: Numerical evidence versus proof
subsection.p: Numerical evidence is useful. It helps us guess patterns. It helps us find examples. It helps us notice mistakes.
But a long list of checked cases is not a proof.

statement.p: The graph of
appears to lie above the x-axis. That suggests q(x)\gt 0 for all real x.
A graph supports the claim, but algebra proves it:
Since (x-1)^2\ge 0, we have (x-1)^2+1\ge 1. Therefore q(x)\ge 1\gt 0 for every real x.
The proof tells us more than the graph. It tells us that the function is not merely positive; it is at least 1.

example.title: A sign change suggests a root

statement.p: Consider
We can compute r(1)=1-1-1=-1 and r(2)=8-2-1=5.
The outputs change from negative to positive between x=1 and x=2. A graph suggests that the curve crosses the x-axis somewhere between them.
Later, after we define continuity, the Intermediate Value Theorem will make this exact. It will say that a continuous function that changes sign on an interval must have a zero inside that interval.
For now, the important lesson is this: numerical evidence gives a clue; a theorem explains when the clue is reliable.

warning.title: Proof warning
warning.p: A computation can show that a statement is true at the inputs tested.
A proof shows why the statement must be true for every allowed input.

subsection.title: A first warning about roundoff
subsection.p: There is another way technology can mislead: numbers are rounded.
A calculator screen may show 10 digits. A computer may store more. But still, it stores only finitely many digits. Most real numbers cannot be stored exactly.
Usually this causes no visible trouble. But when two nearly equal numbers are subtracted, important digits can disappear.

warning.title: Roundoff warning
warning.p: Two algebraically equal formulas can behave differently when approximately computed on a calculator.
The problem is not the mathematics. The problem is the finite storage of decimal or binary approximations.

subsection.p: Calculus is built from small changes:
When h is very small, the numerator often subtracts nearly equal numbers. That makes roundoff error part of the story.
This does not mean we should avoid numerical computation. It means we should understand what the computation is doing.
Sometimes, algebra can make a formula more (numerically) stable. Sometimes a graph needs a better range for variables. Sometimes, a numerical pattern needs a precise definition.
The next chapter provides the missing language. It will make the phrase as x gets close to a into mathematics. That language is the limit.
